summary:
We developed an interactive, full-scale 3D web simulator (`1 unit = 1 km`) of the Sun–Earth–Moon system, built using HTML5, JavaScript (Three.js/WebGL), and PHP, and connected in real time to the **NASA JPL Horizons** API. The model reproduces actual Cartesian `XYZ` coordinates (in the `ICRF` frame), precise polar orientation, lunar libration, and global topography—integrated with a high-resolution stereographic map of the lunar south pole (`80°S–90°S`) based on LROC WAC data.

To address the *New Space Explorers* challenge, the application allows users to select any UTC date or extract time series spanning hundreds of hours (at 10-minute intervals) to animate solar-driven topographic shadows and direct-to-Earth communication coverage—the latter projected in green across the terrain. Clicking on any crater provides its `XYZ` coordinates, altimetry, solar/Earth elevation, and line-of-sight status.

This project is significant because it transforms complex orbital calculations into an intuitive visual tool, enabling mission planners, educators, and the general public to rapidly assess energy-generation windows and direct communication links at the lunar south pole.
Note: The application https://www.ingenieriasygeorradares.com/sistema_lunar_plano/index_v5.html

details:
What benefits does it offer?

Fast and intuitive evaluation: Replaces complex numerical tables with direct spatial visualization, allowing users to compare different landing sites and dates in seconds.

  • Joint power and communications analysis: Enables at-a-glance identification of elevated areas illuminated by the Sun (photovoltaic power potential) that simultaneously maintain a green line-of-sight link to Earth.
  • Universal, zero-install access: Running entirely in a standard web browser with a lightweight architecture, any researcher, student, or member of the public can explore the 3D environment from their computer without installing specialized software or heavy engines.

What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Support for preliminary lunar mission planning: Facilitates the pre-selection of landing zones, rover exploration traverses, and telecommunications relay locations at the lunar south pole, where low Sun and Earth elevation angles make local topography critical.
  • Educational and outreach tool: Helps educators, students, and space enthusiasts visually and rigorously understand concepts such as the ICRF reference frame, lunar libration, permanently shadowed regions (PSRs), and the real geometry of Earth–Moon communication windows.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Programming languages: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES Modules), GLSL (OpenGL Shading Language for topographic vertex and fragment shaders), and PHP 8.
  • Graphics engine and libraries: Three.js (WebGL) featuring logarithmicDepthBuffer for large-scale astronomical precision and camera controls with adaptive continuous zoom.
  • Scientific data and APIs: Official NASA JPL Horizons REST API (ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/api/horizons.api), LRO LOLA global altimetry data, and the LROC WAC polar stereographic mosaic (100 m/pixel, Arizona State University).
  • Infrastructure and deployment: Apache/Linux web server managed via cPanel, utilizing concurrent curl_multi requests in PHP to query ephemerides in real time without relying on external databases.

In what way is your project creative?

  • Visual fusion of power and telecommunications: Translates two complex space engineering challenges—grazing-angle solar irradiance and the Earth–Moon radio-frequency link—into visual layers overlaid directly onto real lunar topography (physics-based shadows + interactive green coverage).
  • Seamless navigation at 1:1 km scale: Integrates both interplanetary distances (149.6 million km to the Sun and 384,400 km to Earth) and the fine topographic detail of kilometer-scale polar craters within a single 3D space using a hybrid mesh (global sphere + co-registered polar stereographic cap).
  • Batch orbital animation player: Incorporates a time-series extractor capable of fetching hundreds of hours of real NASA data in a single query to dynamically observe the shifting of shadows and Earth signal coverage.

What factors did your team take into account?

  • Numerical precision at astronomical scales: In standard WebGL (32-bit), placing objects 150 million kilometers from the origin causes visual jitter. To prevent this, we implemented a 64-bit floating-origin system centered on the observed body combined with a logarithmic depth buffer.
  • True occlusion from terrain relief and curvature: Because the Sun and Earth remain very close to the horizon at the lunar south pole, visibility was not calculated using an ideal sphere alone, but via GPU and CPU topographic raymarching against the elevation profiles of surrounding crater rims.
  • Geometric continuity and performance: We co-registered the altimetric transition between the polar cap (80°S–90°S) and the global sphere to eliminate terrain seams, while optimizing texture memory loading and adding a live diagnostic console alongside an analytical ICRF/IAU fallback to guarantee continuous availability.
